children.text: A small beach town on the west coast between El Nido and Puerto Princesa, with barely a road or a pier, its relaxed pace is the draw. You can swim with sea turtles and island-hop deserted-island beaches much more quietly and cheaply than in El Nido.
Port Barton is a small fishing village in the municipality of San Vicente on the west coast of Palawan. It lies about
150km
by road north of Puerto Princesa and about
150km

by road south of El Nido, so it is a popular rest stop on the route between the two towns. Guesthouses and restaurants line the sandy beach along a crescent-shaped bay, and dozens of islands and coral reefs are scattered offshore.

The village's biggest charm is its slowness. Bangkas beach directly onshore with no pier, and cars are almost nonexistent in the village, so you can walk the sandy paths barefoot. It used to be so remote that electricity from a generator ran only a few hours each evening, and even now that power supply has improved, frequent outages and slow internet naturally impose a kind of digital rest. This atmosphere has made it quietly beloved among European backpackers, who call it "El Nido ten years ago."

The sea is every bit as beautiful as El Nido's. On an island-hopping trip you can cover, in a single day, a seagrass bed where sea turtles often appear, Twin Reef with its healthy coral, shallows scattered with starfish, and small island beaches such as white-sand Exotic Island and Paradise Island. Dozens of tour boats rarely crowd into one spot as they do in El Nido, so you can enjoy it at a relaxed pace.

It suits travelers tired of the crowds at popular destinations, those who want to spend days lying in a hammock reading, and budget-conscious backpackers hoping to enjoy Palawan's sea affordably. It may be less convenient for travelers who need shopping, nightlife, or reliable internet.
The village is said to have originated around
from a place called Itaytay, where ten Tagbanua indigenous households lived, and it grew in the
when loggers arrived. One theory holds that the current name comes from Burton, the name of a British surveyor, as pronounced locally. It became a barangay in
and part of San Vicente when that town was elevated to a municipality in
. As of the
census, the population is about 6,600. Offshore lies the Port Barton Marine Park, managed by the local community. Designated in

, it covers about 123 hectares, and its core zones are the coral reefs of Albaguen Island, Mantaray Reef, and Exotic Island. Because it is a protected area, do not step on or touch the coral, and follow your guide's instructions.

This is a full-day join tour that leaves from the village beach at around 9 AM and returns at around 4 PM. A barbecue lunch and a snorkel mask are included, and the itineraries come in four types, A to D (see the Itinerary tab). Each trip visits 3–5 islands and three or four snorkeling spots, and lunch is often on a small island beach.
In the shallow seagrass beds, you can get a close look at green sea turtles grazing. Keep at least
3m
from a turtle and never touch it.
Twin Reef, where coral splits into two branches, is a snorkeling spot rich in coral and tropical fish. In the shallow water off Starfish Island you can see starfish.

along a path that starts at the north end of the village beach. It takes about
1 hour
on foot, and you can also go by motorbike or tricycle. After signing the guest book at the entrance and paying a donation (usually
15–20 minutes
walk along a forest trail brings you to a pool where you can swim. The trail turns muddy after rain, so you need shoes with good grip, and fewer people go in the morning.
A quiet beach about
30–40 minutes
on foot over the headland south of the village, or about
10 minutes
by bangka. It is a good place to spend half a day in the shade of palm trees.
The village beach faces west, so you can watch the sun set over the sea every evening. Finishing the day with a cocktail in a hammock at a beach restaurant is daily life in Port Barton.
Rent one on the beach and paddle out across the calm bay toward a nearby island or the mangroves.

The nearest major airport is Puerto Princesa International Airport (PPS), about
1 hour 20 minutes
from Manila, at around

one way. San Vicente also has a small airport, but scheduled flights are irregular, so most travelers use Puerto Princesa. You can also fly into El Nido Airport (ENI) and travel down after finishing your El Nido trip.
Since
March 29, 2026

, direct flights to El Nido Airport depart from Clark, Cebu, Boracay (Caticlan), and elsewhere instead of Manila. If departing from Manila, the Puerto Princesa route is the most convenient and cheapest.
A shared van from Puerto Princesa Airport or the Irawan terminal to Port Barton takes about
3–4 hours
and costs about

. You can book a lodging pickup, and the van runs along the national highway toward Roxas and turns onto the western mountain road near Salvacion; this section is fully paved now, so travel is much easier than before. Taking a Roxas-bound bus and transferring to a jeepney or motorcycle at the Salvacion junction is cheaper but takes much longer. From El Nido it is about
4–5 hours
by shared van, about
Puerto Princesa's city integrated terminal moved in

from San Jose in the north of the city to Irawan in the south, so going to Port Barton, which is to the north, means a detour. Boarding directly at the airport or booking a lodging pickup saves time. Vans to Port Barton leave only a few times a day (around morning, noon, and afternoon), so it is best to book the day before and reconfirm the departure time.

A boat trip hopping between islands along the coast sometimes operates between El Nido and Port Barton. Whether it's running depends on the weather and the operator, so check locally.
You can walk everywhere within the village. For the waterfall or Long Beach direction, rent a motorbike (about
per day) or negotiate with a tricycle or motorbike driver.
From Puerto Princesa, you drive about
120km
on the national highway toward Roxas and then about
23km
up the western mountain road, about
146km
in total, which takes
3–4 hours

. Most of it is paved, but in the rainy season it is best to check the condition of the mountain road in advance. Riding a rented motorbike all the way takes 4–5 hours and is tiring; within the village, a motorbike or walking is more convenient.
November
through
May
is the dry season and good for visiting.
March
through
May
especially has the calmest sea and clearest water, the best time for island hopping and snorkeling. From
December
to
February
there are some windy days, but the cool temperatures make it good for trekking.
Port Barton is on the west coast, so it takes the full effect of the southwest monsoon Habagat from
June
to
October

. In this period, high waves often cancel island hopping or limit it to nearby islands only, and rain slows travel on the mountain road too. On the plus side, lodging is cheaper and the village gets even quieter. If you visit during the rainy season, it's best to schedule island hopping with some flexibility.
Peak season is
late December
through New Year and
January–March
. In this period the sea is calmest and rainfall is lowest, so rooms fill quickly and island-hopping bookings pile up. Sea turtles can be seen most consistently from
December–May
, and the water off the village beach is calmest before
. During Holy Week (around
March 25–28

in 2027), domestic Filipino travelers flood in and lodging runs short, so book one to two months ahead. Because Port Barton is on the west coast, even when no typhoon is passing, there are days when the Coast Guard blocks departures because of waves out at sea.

Lodging centers on guesthouses and bungalows lining the village beach. A backpacker dorm runs about
per night, a fan bungalow about
, and an air-conditioned beach bungalow or small resort about

. A spot right on the beach gets the best sunset views but can have restaurant noise in the evening, while the village interior is quieter and cheaper. For somewhere even more secluded, you can choose a resort on a nearby island reached by bangka, or around White Beach. Rooms fill up fast in peak season, so book ahead.

The food centers on fresh seafood barbecue at beach restaurants. In the evening, beach restaurants grill the day's catch of fish, squid, and shrimp over charcoal, and many also serve dishes like coconut curry and seafood pasta suited to Western travelers' tastes. Small Filipino restaurants in the village serve home-style dishes like adobo, sinigang, and pancit for about
per person. A few European-run bakeries and cafes are good for breakfast too. Island-hopping lunches typically feature grilled fish, pork, rice, and fruit served on a deserted-island beach.

Few lodgings have air-conditioned rooms, so confirm when booking, and some lodgings run Wi-Fi and electricity only at set hours. Backpacker places such as Cocorico Hostel (dorms) and Russell's Place have operated along the village beach for years, and beach bungalows such as Ausan Beach Front Cottages sit right on the beach. For restaurants, Gakayan, known for cheap local food and seafood, and Reef Cafe, known for its handmade burgers, are consistently recommended. A seafood main dish is usually around
, and many places take cash only.
The village has no ATM, or one that's often out of order, and cards are almost never accepted. Bring enough cash from Puerto Princesa or El Nido to cover your whole stay.
Power has improved but outages are still frequent, so it's a good idea to bring a power bank and a flashlight.
The internet is slow and unstable, so if you have work or urgent calls to make, bring SIM cards from both Smart and Globe, and handle anything important before you arrive.
You can book island hopping at a tour booth on the beach or through your accommodation on your first day, for departure the next day. It's worth comparing routes and inclusions across a few booths.
Bangkas beach directly on the sand, so you'll wade in up to your knees when boarding or disembarking. Pack your belongings in a dry bag.
At night, the beach and lanes have little lighting, so a flashlight comes in handy.
Local guides say your odds of meeting a sea turtle are best in the morning.

On days when the Coast Guard blocks sailing to the open sea, island hopping is sometimes run on a changed course to calm spots inside the bay. When booking, it is a good idea to ask about the alternative course and the cancellation and refund terms.
On arrival, you pay the environmental registration fee of
at the village tourism desk and receive a card. It is valid for about
10 days
and must be shown on island-hopping trips, so keep it safe.
A round trip by bangka to White Beach or Coconut Beach costs about
, and if you go before
the sea is calm and there are fewer people.
Touching, chasing, or riding a sea turtle is prohibited and can carry a penalty if caught. Follow your guide's instructions and keep your distance while observing.
Wear a life vest on the bangka, and don't insist on going out on high-wave days.
The beach sand has many sand flies, and a bite can itch severely for days, so bring insect repellent.
The nearest large hospital is in Puerto Princesa, several hours away. Bring basic medicine and travel insurance.
Environmental fee and tour rules can change by decision of the San Vicente tourism office, so check the latest notices.
In the rainy season, landslides or washed-out roads can occur on the mountain road, so check road conditions before traveling.
The waterfall trail turns muddy after rain and the mossy rocks are slippery, so wear shoes with good grip rather than sandals.
